details:
**Goliath**
David's most famous deed and the usual giveaway. As a young shepherd, David refused to wear King Saul's armor and faced the Philistine giant Goliath, who came armed with a sword, spear, and javelin, in the Valley of Elah. Taking five smooth stones, he killed Goliath with a single stone from his sling.

**Bathsheba and Uriah the Hittite**
After seeing Bathsheba bathing, David committed adultery with her and got her pregnant. He then had her husband Uriah the Hittite, a soldier in his army, placed in the front lines of battle so that he would be killed, and married Bathsheba, who later bore him Solomon. Matthew's genealogy of Jesus refers to her only as "the wife of Uriah."

**Nathan's rebuke**
The prophet Nathan confronted David over the death of Uriah with a parable about a rich man who takes a poor man's only ewe lamb. The Qur'an has a parallel story in which David (Dawud) is interrupted at prayer by two men arguing over ewes and realizes God is rebuking him.

**Michal and the dowry of Philistine foreskins**
King Saul demanded a hundred Philistine foreskins as the bride price for his daughter Michal, hoping David would die trying. David brought back two hundred. Michal later rebuked David for dancing publicly before the Ark of the Covenant and, as a consequence, died childless.

**Son of Jesse anointed by Samuel**
David was the youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem and was anointed king by the prophet Samuel while working as a shepherd. When Samuel was impressed by David's older brothers, God told him that "man looks at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart."

**Author of the Psalms**
David is traditionally credited with writing many of the Psalms. As a youth he entered Saul's service by soothing the troubled king with his lyre (harp), and New Testament writers often quote messianic Psalms attributed to him, such as Psalm 110.

**Absalom's rebellion**
David's son Absalom led a rebellion that forced David to flee Jerusalem. Absalom died after his long hair got caught in the branches of a tree, after which David's general Joab killed him.

**Jonathan**
The son of King Saul and David's closest friend. When Saul plotted to kill David, Jonathan warned him by deliberately shooting an arrow past a boy as a prearranged signal to flee.

**Father of Solomon and the Temple**
David was succeeded by his son Solomon, whose mother was Bathsheba. David wanted to build a temple for God in Jerusalem, but because he was a man of war, God forbade it, and Solomon built the First Temple instead.

**Second king of Israel and successor to Saul**
David succeeded Saul as king of Israel. He fought a war against Saul's son Ish-bosheth, which turned in his favor when Saul's general Abner defected, and he captured Jerusalem, making it his capital, the "City of David."

**Feigning madness before Achish of Gath**
While fleeing Saul, David took refuge with the Philistine king Achish of Gath, where he pretended to be insane, scratching at doors and letting saliva run down his beard, to escape danger. A Jewish legend says David did not understand the purpose of spiders, mosquitoes, or madness until each saved his life.

**Sparing Saul's life**
While hiding from Saul in the wilderness, including at the Cave of Adullam, David had chances to kill his father-in-law but spared him. Once, finding Saul relieving himself in a cave, David only cut off a corner of Saul's robe.

**Amnon and Tamar**
David's son Amnon raped his half-sister Tamar, David's daughter. Her full brother Absalom later had Amnon killed in revenge, beginning the feud among David's sons.

**Joab and David's mighty men**
Joab commanded David's army and helped carry out Uriah's death; on his deathbed David told Solomon to punish Joab, who had murdered the commander Amasa. When three of David's warriors risked their lives to bring him water from the well of Bethlehem, he poured it on the ground, calling it "the blood of men who went at the risk of their lives."

**Ancestor of the Messiah**
Jewish tradition holds that the Messiah will descend from David, and the New Testament calls Jesus the "Son of David" and refers to Bethlehem as the "city of David." In the Qur'an, God teaches David how to make chain mail.
